title: Retroperitoneum & Posterior Abdominal Wall
summary: Study the organs and structures behind the peritoneum: kidneys, adrenals, ureters, great vessels and the lumbar plexus.

lessons.title: Kidneys, Renal Fascia and Perirenal Spaces

levels.kid:
Your two **kidneys** are shaped like beans, each about as big as your fist. They sit high up in your back, one on each side of your spine, tucked just under your lowest ribs.

They are not floating loose. Each kidney is wrapped in layers, like a gift. First there is a tight skin around the kidney. Then comes a soft blanket of **fat**. Around the fat is a thin bag that holds everything together.

The fat is like bubble wrap. It cushions the kidney when you jump and run.

The right kidney sits a little lower than the left. Why? A big organ called the liver sits on top of it and pushes it down a bit.
levels.hs:
The **kidneys** are paired organs that filter blood and make urine. Each is about 11 cm long. They lie in the **retroperitoneum**, the space behind the peritoneum, which is the slippery lining of the abdominal cavity. They sit against the back muscles at roughly the level of vertebrae T12 to L3.

The kidneys sit in layers. From the inside out:
- **Renal capsule**: a tough fibrous coat stuck tightly to the kidney.
- **Perirenal (perinephric) fat**: a fat cushion that also surrounds the adrenal gland.
- **Renal fascia** (Gerota's fascia): a sheet of connective tissue that encloses the kidney, its fat and the adrenal gland.
- **Pararenal fat**: more fat outside the fascia, thickest at the back.

On the inner, concave edge of each kidney is the **hilum**. This is where the renal vein, renal artery and renal pelvis enter or leave. From front to back they run in that order, vein, artery, pelvis, which you can remember as "VAP."

The right kidney sits about 1 to 2 cm lower than the left because the liver lies above it. Both kidneys move a few centimetres when you breathe, because the diaphragm pushes them down on each breath in.

Real example: a kidney injury from a fall can bleed, and the renal fascia often holds that blood near the kidney, which helps limit the bleeding.
levels.college:
**Position and relations.** The kidneys lie in the paravertebral gutters on psoas major (medially), quadratus lumborum and the transversus abdominis aponeurosis. The left extends from about T11/T12 to L2/L3. The right is about one vertebra lower. Rib 12 crosses the posterior surface of each kidney. The diaphragm separates the upper pole from the **costodiaphragmatic recess** of the pleura, so a posterior approach can enter the pleura by mistake. The kidney hila face anteromedially, around L1 (the transpyloric plane).

Anterior relations:
- **Right**: liver (via the hepatorenal pouch of Morison), descending duodenum (part 2) medially, right colic flexure.
- **Left**: stomach, spleen, pancreatic tail and splenic vessels, jejunum, left colic flexure.

**Internal structure.** The outer cortex contains glomeruli and dips between pyramids as renal columns. The medulla's pyramids drain through papillae into minor calyces, then major calyces, then the renal pelvis, then the ureter. The **renal sinus** is the fat-filled space inside the hilum.

**Segmental arteries.** Each renal artery divides into anterior and posterior divisions, which give about five segmental arteries (apical, superior, middle, inferior and posterior). These are **end arteries**, so blocking one causes a wedge of infarction. The plane between the anterior and posterior territories is **Brödel's line**, a relatively avascular zone just behind the lateral border. The veins, by contrast, connect freely with each other.

**Fascia and spaces.** The renal fascia has two layers. The anterior layer is called Gerota's; the posterior layer is called Zuckerkandl's. They enclose the **perirenal space**. Outside them lie the **anterior pararenal space** (containing the pancreas, duodenum parts 2 to 4, and the ascending and descending colon) and the **posterior pararenal space** (fat only). Laterally the two layers fuse into the **lateroconal fascia**. The perirenal space is closed at the top, and it is weak or open at the bottom along the ureter.
levels.phd:
The classic **three-compartment model** of Meyers (1970s), worked out using CT and contrast injections into cadavers, divides the extraperitoneal space into anterior pararenal, perirenal and posterior pararenal spaces. It explains why disease spreads along predictable routes:
- Pancreatitis fluid collects first in the anterior pararenal space and tends to track along the lateroconal fascia, rather than into the perirenal space.
- The perirenal space is cone-shaped. Superiorly it is tethered to the diaphragmatic fascia. Inferiorly its layers merge loosely with the periureteric tissue and iliac fascia. As a result, perinephric collections can spread toward the pelvis.
- Whether the left and right perirenal spaces communicate across the midline, around the aorta and IVC, is disputed. Contrast studies show that limited communication is possible in a minority of cases.

**Interfascial planes** (Molmenti; Raptopoulos; Gore). Modern work treats the renal fascia as laminated rather than a single sheet. Potential spaces open inside it, namely the retromesenteric, retrorenal and lateroconal planes, and they join across the midline. Fluid from rapidly spreading pancreatitis or a bleeding aneurysm dissects through these planes rather than filling only the three classic boxes. This explains why perirenal-like collections appear in places Meyers' model did not predict.

Within the perirenal space, **bridging septa** run from the renal capsule to the fascia. Some septa form channels that drain lymph and carry the subcapsular arteries. Fluid can travel along them, and the septa also limit how far a subcapsular haematoma spreads.

**Renal vasculature.** Graves' 1954 corrosion-cast studies defined the five segmental arteries. The posterior segmental artery passes behind the renal pelvis, so a posterior pyelotomy can injure it. Accessory (polar) renal arteries occur in roughly a quarter to a third of kidneys. They are persistent embryonic branches left over from the kidney's ascent, and they enter the poles directly. A lower-pole vessel crossing the pelviureteric junction is a recognised cause of extrinsic obstruction there.

The kidney's ascent from the pelvis, together with its medial rotation, explains why the hilum faces anteromedially. Failure of either process leads to pelvic kidney or malrotation.
levels.expert:
**Imaging and interventional relevance.** On CT, a thickened renal fascia is a nonspecific but useful sign of inflammation or tumour invasion. Fat stranding confined to the perirenal space points toward a renal source, such as pyelonephritis or a forniceal rupture from obstruction. Stranding in the anterior pararenal space points toward the pancreas or colon. Perirenal gas suggests emphysematous pyelonephritis, a surgical emergency typically seen in patients with diabetes.

**Staging.** In the AJCC TNM system, renal cell carcinoma that invades perirenal fat but stays within Gerota's fascia is **T3a**. Spread beyond Gerota's fascia, including contiguous adrenal invasion, is **T4**. This is why radical nephrectomy is performed *outside* the fascia, removing the kidney with its fat envelope intact. Partial nephrectomy depends on segmental anatomy. Selective clamping of the segmental arteries, often guided by 3D CT reconstruction, aims to reduce warm ischaemia to the healthy parenchyma.

**Percutaneous access.** For percutaneous nephrolithotomy, the puncture is placed through a posterior calyx along Brödel's avascular plane, entering via the papilla rather than the infundibulum to avoid the interlobar vessels. Upper-pole access above rib 12 or rib 11 risks entering the pleura, because the costodiaphragmatic recess lies behind the upper pole. A **retrorenal colon**, present more often in thin, elderly or prone patients, can be perforated during this approach. Prone CT planning helps identify it.

**Trauma.** The AAST grading system for renal injury was revised in 2018. A perirenal haematoma contained by Gerota's fascia may tamponade itself, which supports nonoperative management in haemodynamically stable patients. Surgically opening the fascia can release that tamponade. Active contrast extravasation is treated preferentially with angioembolisation.

**Page kidney.** A chronic subcapsular haematoma, or a fibrous perirenal shell, compresses the kidney. This reduces renal perfusion, which activates the renin system and causes hypertension. The condition was first described experimentally by Irvine Page in 1939, who wrapped kidneys in cellophane to produce it.

**Open questions.** The exact lamination of the renal fascia remains debated. So does whether the left and right perirenal spaces truly communicate across the midline. These questions matter for predicting how a collection will spread, and for robotic retroperitoneal surgery, where the fascial planes are used to find the route of dissection.

keyPoints: Kidneys are retroperitoneal, about T12-L3, with the right lower than the left because of the liver
Layers from inside out: capsule, perirenal fat, renal (Gerota's) fascia, pararenal fat
Hilar structures from anterior to posterior: renal vein, artery, pelvis
Segmental renal arteries are end arteries; Brödel's line is a relatively avascular plane
Meyers' three spaces: anterior pararenal, perirenal and posterior pararenal
Perirenal space is closed superiorly and weak inferiorly along the ureter

test.q: Which layer lies immediately outside the renal capsule?
test.explain: The order from inside out is capsule, then perirenal fat, then renal fascia, then pararenal fat.

test.q: From anterior to posterior, the structures at the renal hilum are:
test.explain: Vein, artery, pelvis, which is remembered as VAP.

test.q: Why does the right kidney usually sit lower than the left?
choices: The aorta lies to its right
The psoas muscle is shorter there
test.explain: The large right lobe of the liver displaces the right kidney inferiorly by about 1 to 2 cm.

test.q: Which organ lies in the anterior pararenal space?
test.explain: The pancreas, duodenum and ascending/descending colon occupy the anterior pararenal space. The adrenal gland lies in the perirenal space with the kidney.

test.q: Segmental renal arteries are clinically important because they are:
test.explain: Segmental arteries are end arteries, so blocking one causes a wedge infarct. The renal veins, unlike the arteries, anastomose freely.

test.q: A posterior approach to the upper pole of the kidney risks entering the:
choices: Right paracolic gutter of the peritoneum
test.explain: The pleural costodiaphragmatic recess lies behind the upper pole, beyond the diaphragm.

test.q: The perirenal space is weakest or open in which direction?
test.explain: It is tethered superiorly to the diaphragmatic fascia and merges loosely inferiorly along the ureter, so collections can track toward the pelvis.

test.q: Which structure is an anterior relation of the left kidney?
test.explain: The pancreatic tail and splenic vessels lie in front of the left kidney. The other three are right-sided relations.

test.q: Which muscle lies directly medial to the kidney on the posterior wall?
test.explain: The kidney rests on psoas major medially and quadratus lumborum more laterally.

test.q: What eponym is commonly given to the renal fascia (or its anterior layer)?
test.explain: Gerota's fascia encloses the kidney, the perirenal fat and the adrenal gland.

test.q: The fat-filled space inside the hilum, holding the calyces and vessels, is the renal ___.
test.explain: The renal sinus is the space within the kidney entered through the hilum.

test.q: The relatively avascular plane between anterior and posterior arterial territories is called ___'s line.
test.explain: Brödel's line lies just behind the lateral border of the kidney and is used for incisions and access.

kidTest.q: What shape is a kidney?
kidTest.explain: Kidneys are bean-shaped.

kidTest.q: Where are your kidneys?
choices: Down in your legs, near your knees
Inside your head, behind your eyes
In your back, under your ribs
kidTest.explain: They sit high in the back, on each side of the spine.

kidTest.q: What does the fat around the kidney do?
choices: Makes it beat like a heart
kidTest.explain: The fat protects the kidney when you move.

kidTest.q: Why is the right kidney a little lower?
choices: The liver sits on top of it
kidTest.explain: The big liver presses the right kidney down a little.

kidTest.q: Each kidney is about as big as your f _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: A kidney is roughly fist-sized.

advancedTest.q: A renal tumour invades perirenal fat but stays within the renal fascia. Why is radical nephrectomy done outside the fascia?
choices: Extrafascial dissection lets the surgeon avoid the hilum
Removing the intact fascial envelope clears the invaded fat
Keeping the fascia in place protects the adrenal gland
The fascia is the main blood supply to the tumour
advancedTest.explain: Perirenal fat invasion (T3a) is contained by Gerota's fascia, so removing the kidney within its intact fascial envelope removes the disease.

advancedTest.q: CT shows fluid tracking along the lateroconal fascia, sparing the perirenal fat. The most likely source is:
advancedTest.explain: Pancreatitis fluid fills the anterior pararenal space and spreads along the lateroconal fascia. Renal and adrenal sources fill the perirenal space.

advancedTest.q: Why might surgical exploration worsen a stable perirenal haematoma after trauma?
choices: It allows urine to enter the peritoneal cavity
Opening the fascia releases its tamponading effect
It disrupts Brödel's line and causes infarction
It exposes the segmental veins to air embolism
advancedTest.explain: The renal fascia contains the bleed and can tamponade it. Opening the fascia removes that containment.

advancedTest.q: A perinephric abscess later appears in the pelvis. The best anatomical explanation is that the perirenal space:
choices: Opens into the posterior mediastinum above
Communicates freely with the lesser sac
Merges loosely with periureteric tissue below
Drains through the renal sinus to the bladder
advancedTest.explain: The perirenal cone is fixed superiorly but weak inferiorly along the ureter and iliac fascia, which allows spread toward the pelvis.

lessons.title: Adrenal Glands: Relations and Triple Arterial Supply

levels.kid:
On top of each kidney sits a small gland called the **adrenal gland**. It looks like a little hat. You have two, one on each side.

These tiny glands make important messengers called **hormones**. One of them is adrenaline. It makes your heart beat fast when you get a big fright.

The adrenal glands are small but very busy, so they need lots of blood. They get it from three different pipes. Think of a house with three water taps instead of one. If one tap is slow, the others still help.

But only one main pipe carries the used blood away. So the drain pipe has to work hard.
levels.hs:
The **adrenal glands** (also called **suprarenal glands**, meaning "above the kidney") are two small endocrine glands, each weighing only about 4 to 5 grams. They sit on the upper inner pole of each kidney. They lie in the **retroperitoneum**, the space behind the lining of the abdomen.

Each gland has two parts:
- The **cortex** (outer layer) makes steroid hormones such as cortisol and aldosterone.
- The **medulla** (inner core) makes adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline.

The two glands differ in shape:
- The **right** adrenal is **pyramid-shaped**. It sits tucked behind the inferior vena cava (IVC), the large vein returning blood to the heart.
- The **left** adrenal is **crescent-shaped** and sits closer to the aorta, behind the stomach and pancreas.

The adrenals have a **triple arterial supply**. On each side there are three sets of arteries:
- **Superior suprarenal arteries**, from the inferior phrenic artery
- **Middle suprarenal artery**, straight from the aorta
- **Inferior suprarenal artery**, from the renal artery

In contrast, each gland drains through a **single suprarenal vein**. The right vein empties directly into the IVC. The left vein empties into the left renal vein.

Real example: when surgeons remove an adrenal tumor, finding and tying off that single vein is one of the key steps.
levels.college:
The suprarenal glands are retroperitoneal endocrine organs enclosed within the **renal (Gerota's) fascia**. A thin septum of fascia separates each gland from its kidney. Because of that septum, the adrenal usually stays in place when the kidney is ectopic or removed.

**Relations of the right adrenal** (pyramidal):
- Anteromedially: the **IVC**. The gland is partly hidden behind it.
- Anterolaterally: the bare area of the **liver**.
- Posteriorly: the right crus and the posterior part of the **diaphragm**.
- Inferiorly: the upper pole of the right kidney.

**Relations of the left adrenal** (crescentic, extending down the medial border of the kidney toward the hilum):
- Anteriorly: the **stomach**, with the **omental bursa** (lesser sac) between, plus the **pancreas** and **splenic artery**.
- Medially: the left crus of the diaphragm and the celiac ganglion.
- Posteriorly: the diaphragm.

**Arterial supply (triple, per side):**
- **Superior suprarenal arteries**: several small branches of the **inferior phrenic artery**
- **Middle suprarenal artery**: a direct branch of the **abdominal aorta** near the level of the superior mesenteric artery
- **Inferior suprarenal artery**: from the **renal artery**

These arteries break into many fine twigs that enter the gland around its periphery. They form a **subcapsular plexus** that feeds sinusoids running through the cortex toward the medulla.

**Venous drainage** is through one central **suprarenal vein** emerging at the **hilum**:
- The right vein is very short and enters the **posterior IVC** directly.
- The left vein is longer and joins the **left renal vein**, often after merging with the left inferior phrenic vein.

**Innervation**: preganglionic sympathetic fibers, mainly via the **thoracic splanchnic nerves** through the celiac plexus, synapse directly on **chromaffin cells** of the medulla. Embryologically these cells are modified postganglionic neurons of neural crest origin. The cortex arises from coelomic mesoderm.
levels.phd:
The adrenal's vascular architecture is functionally important, not just anatomical trivia. Arterial blood reaches the gland through about 50 to 60 small capsular arteries, which come from the three suprarenal sources. These form a **capsular plexus** that gives rise to two circuits:
- **Cortical sinusoids**, which run centripetally through the zona glomerulosa, fasciculata and reticularis.
- A minority of **medullary arteries**, which pass directly to the medulla.

The cortical sinusoids drain into medullary venules. As a result, chromaffin cells are bathed in blood carrying very high glucocorticoid concentrations. Cortisol induces **phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT)**, the enzyme that converts noradrenaline to adrenaline. This **corticomedullary portal-like arrangement** explains why the adrenal medulla is the body's main source of circulating adrenaline. Extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue, such as the paraganglia, secretes mostly noradrenaline. Wurtman and Axelrod's 1960s work showed that hypophysectomy reduces PNMT and that glucocorticoids restore it.

The central vein has unusual **longitudinal bundles of smooth muscle** in its wall that are eccentrically arranged. Contraction of these bundles may regulate outflow and the residence time of hormones within the gland.

The arterial pattern is highly variable. The middle suprarenal artery may be absent, multiple or bilateral-asymmetric. The inferior suprarenal artery may come from an accessory renal or gonadal artery. Rich anastomoses between the three sources make arterial occlusion rarely infarctive.

The venous pattern is the weak point. A single draining vein, combined with dense capsular arterial inflow, creates a classic **vascular dam**. If venous outflow is obstructed, as in thrombosis, high arterial inflow continues. This predisposes the gland to **hemorrhagic infarction**. That mechanism underlies adrenal hemorrhage in anticoagulated patients, in antiphospholipid syndrome, and in **Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome**, classically seen with meningococcal sepsis.

The asymmetry of the two veins also matters for physiology. The left suprarenal vein joins the left renal vein, so left-sided adrenal and renal venous pressures are coupled. The right vein does not share this link.
levels.expert:
Clinically, the asymmetric venous anatomy dominates adrenal surgery and interventional practice.

**Adrenal vein sampling (AVS)** is the reference standard for lateralizing primary aldosteronism. It distinguishes a unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma, which is surgically curable, from bilateral hyperplasia, which is treated medically. CT alone misclassifies lateralization in a substantial minority of patients, particularly older ones with incidental nonfunctioning nodules.
- Cannulating the **left vein** is relatively easy through the left renal vein, typically at the common trunk with the inferior phrenic vein.
- Cannulating the **right vein** is the main technical hurdle. The vein is short and enters the posterior IVC at an acute angle, sometimes from an accessory hepatic vein.
- A **selectivity index** confirms correct catheter placement. It compares adrenal-vein cortisol with peripheral cortisol.

**Adrenalectomy**, whether laparoscopic transperitoneal or **posterior retroperitoneoscopic adrenalectomy (PRA)**, follows anatomy-driven principles:
- On the **right**, the short vein draining into the IVC risks torrential bleeding or IVC tear. Early identification by medial retraction of the liver is key.
- On the **left**, the vein is followed along the left renal vein.
- In **pheochromocytoma**, surgeons classically ligate the vein early to limit catecholamine surges during handling. Some now argue this matters less with modern alpha-blockade, so the point remains debated.
- The arteries are small and are usually controlled with energy devices rather than individually.

**Pitfalls**:
- A **left renal vein** that runs behind the aorta, or circles it, alters the AVS approach and the course of dissection.
- An enlarged right adrenal mass can push into the bare area of the liver and mimic a hepatic lesion on imaging.
- Normal adrenal limbs normally measure under about 10 mm in thickness. Bilateral enlargement should prompt consideration of hyperplasia, metastasis or hemorrhage.

**Advances and open questions**:
- **Segmental AVS**, which samples the central-vein tributaries, supports **partial adrenalectomy** for bilateral disease.
- Molecular subtyping, such as **KCNJ5** mutations and **CYP11B2** immunostaining, is reframing what counts as unilateral disease.
- Imaging alternatives such as **11C-metomidate** and **CXCR4-targeted PET** may eventually reduce reliance on invasive sampling.

keyPoints: Adrenals are retroperitoneal, inside renal fascia, on the superomedial kidney poles
Right adrenal is pyramidal and lies behind the IVC; left is crescentic, behind stomach and pancreas
Superior suprarenal arteries come from the inferior phrenic artery
Middle suprarenal comes from the aorta; inferior suprarenal comes from the renal artery
One vein per side: right to the IVC, left to the left renal vein
Many arteries but one vein predisposes the gland to hemorrhagic infarction

test.q: The superior suprarenal arteries arise from which vessel?
test.explain: The superior suprarenal arteries are several small branches of the inferior phrenic artery. The renal artery gives the inferior suprarenal artery instead.

test.q: The middle suprarenal artery is a branch of the:
test.explain: It arises directly from the abdominal aorta, near the level of the superior mesenteric artery.

test.q: Where does the left suprarenal vein usually drain?
test.explain: The left suprarenal vein joins the left renal vein. The right suprarenal vein drains directly into the IVC.

test.q: Which structure lies anteromedial to the right adrenal gland?
test.explain: The right adrenal is tucked partly behind the IVC. The stomach and pancreas are anterior relations of the left gland.

test.q: What shape is the left adrenal gland typically described as?
test.explain: The left adrenal is crescent-shaped and extends down the medial kidney border. The right adrenal is pyramidal.

test.q: The adrenal medulla secretes mainly:
test.explain: Chromaffin cells of the medulla make adrenaline and noradrenaline. Cortisol and aldosterone come from the cortex.

test.q: Why does the adrenal usually stay in place when the kidney is removed?
choices: Its arteries anchor it to the spine
A fascial septum separates it from the kidney
It is attached firmly to the liver
It lies inside the peritoneal cavity
test.explain: Within the renal fascia, a thin septum divides the adrenal from the kidney, so the gland stays put.

test.q: Which relation is anterior to the left adrenal gland, across the lesser sac?
test.explain: The stomach lies anterior to the left adrenal, with the omental bursa (lesser sac) in between. The liver's bare area relates to the right gland.

test.q: The medulla's preganglionic sympathetic input arrives mainly through the:
test.explain: Thoracic splanchnic nerves bring preganglionic fibers that synapse directly on the chromaffin cells.

test.q: The lowest of the three arteries feeding each gland above the kidney branches from the ___ artery.
test.explain: The renal artery gives off the inferior suprarenal artery.

test.q: What other name for the adrenal glands means 'above the kidney'?
test.explain: 'Suprarenal' means above the kidney.

test.q: The adrenals lie behind the peritoneum, in the ___.
test.explain: They are retroperitoneal organs enclosed within the renal fascia.

kidTest.q: Where does the adrenal gland sit?
kidTest.explain: It sits on top of each kidney, like a little hat.

kidTest.q: Which hormone helps your heart beat fast when you are scared?
kidTest.explain: The adrenal gland makes adrenaline.

kidTest.q: How many adrenal glands do you have?
kidTest.explain: You have two, one on each kidney.

kidTest.q: How many main pipes bring blood to each adrenal gland?
kidTest.explain: Three different arteries bring blood in.

kidTest.q: Adrenal glands make chemical messengers called h _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Hormones are messengers that travel in the blood.

advancedTest.q: Why is adrenaline, rather than noradrenaline, the main product of the adrenal medulla?
choices: Medullary arteries deliver tyrosine at much higher levels
The central vein's smooth muscle methylates noradrenaline
Splanchnic nerves release adrenaline directly into the gland
Cortisol-rich sinusoidal blood induces PNMT in chromaffin cells
advancedTest.explain: Cortical sinusoids drain toward the medulla, exposing chromaffin cells to high cortisol. Cortisol induces PNMT, which converts noradrenaline to adrenaline.

advancedTest.q: Adrenal vein thrombosis tends to cause hemorrhagic infarction because:
choices: Chromaffin cells release anticoagulants when their blood supply drops
Arterial inflow continues while the single venous outflow is blocked
The cortex lacks capillaries and relies on diffusion from the capsule
The three arterial sources rarely anastomose with each other
advancedTest.explain: Rich capsular arterial inflow drains through one vein. When that vein is blocked, the gland engorges and bleeds, like a dammed river.

advancedTest.q: During adrenal vein sampling, which side is usually harder to cannulate, and why?
choices: The left, because its vein drains into the splenic vein
The right, because it joins the right renal vein
The right, because its short vein enters the posterior IVC
The left, because its vein passes behind the aorta
advancedTest.explain: The right suprarenal vein is short and enters the back of the IVC at an acute angle. The left vein is reached easily through the left renal vein.

advancedTest.q: In a patient with a retroaortic left renal vein, adrenal vein sampling on the left is complicated mainly because:
choices: The left gland becomes pyramidal and lies behind the IVC
The left suprarenal vein then drains into the hepatic veins
The middle suprarenal artery is displaced over the vein
The route to the left suprarenal vein through its renal vein is altered
advancedTest.explain: The left suprarenal vein drains into the left renal vein. If that vein runs behind the aorta, the catheter path to the adrenal vein changes.

lessons.title: Ureters: Course, Constrictions and Relations

levels.kid:
Your kidneys clean your blood and make pee. But the pee has to travel down to your bladder. It goes through two thin tubes called **ureters**, one from each kidney.

Each ureter is about as long as a ruler and thinner than a pencil. It doesn't just let pee drip down. Its walls squeeze in waves, like you squeezing toothpaste along a tube. That is why pee can move even when you lie down!

The ureter has three narrow spots, like tight parts of a garden hose. A tiny hard stone, called a kidney stone, can get stuck there. That hurts a lot.

Surgeons are careful near the ureters, because these tubes pass very close to big blood vessels deep in the belly.
levels.hs:
The **ureters** are paired muscular tubes that carry urine from each kidney to the urinary bladder. Each is about 25-30 cm long and a few millimetres wide. They lie in the **retroperitoneum**, meaning behind the peritoneum, the membrane lining the abdominal cavity.

Urine does not simply fall down the ureter. Smooth muscle in the wall contracts in waves called **peristalsis**, pushing urine along a few times per minute.

Each ureter begins at the **renal pelvis**, a funnel inside the kidney. It runs down on the psoas muscle, crosses into the pelvis, and enters the back of the bladder at an angle.

The ureter is narrowest at three places, the **constrictions**:
- the **pelviureteric junction**, where the renal pelvis becomes the ureter
- where it crosses the **pelvic brim**, over the iliac vessels
- the **vesicoureteric junction**, where it passes through the bladder wall

These are where **kidney stones** most often lodge. A trapped stone causes **renal colic**, severe pain that comes in waves and spreads from the flank toward the groin.

Real example: in women, the ureter passes just under the uterine artery near the cervix, a famous relation summed up as "water under the bridge." Surgeons doing a hysterectomy must protect it.
levels.college:
**Course.** Each ureter (about 25-30 cm) has an abdominal part and a pelvic part of roughly equal length. It leaves the **renal pelvis** at the pelviureteric junction (PUJ), near the level of L1-L2, and descends on the anterior surface of **psoas major**. On radiographs it roughly follows the tips of the lumbar transverse processes. It enters the pelvis by crossing the **bifurcation of the common iliac artery** (or the start of the external iliac) at the pelvic brim. It then runs posteroinferiorly on the lateral pelvic wall, anterior to the internal iliac artery, before turning medially at the level of the ischial spine to reach the bladder.

**Constrictions** (common stone sites):
- PUJ
- pelvic brim (crossing of the iliac vessels)
- vesicoureteric junction (VUJ), the narrowest. Here the ureter runs obliquely through the detrusor, creating a flap-valve that resists reflux.

**Abdominal relations.** The ureter is retroperitoneal and adheres to the posterior parietal peritoneum. It is crossed anteriorly by the **gonadal vessels**. On the right it lies behind the duodenum (2nd part), the right colic and ileocolic vessels, and the root of the mesentery. On the left it lies behind the left colic vessels and the sigmoid mesocolon. In both sexes the ureter passes deep to the vessels that run toward the gut and gonads.

**Pelvic relations.**
- Female: lies about 1-2 cm lateral to the cervix, passing **inferior to the uterine artery** in the base of the broad ligament.
- Male: crossed superiorly by the **ductus deferens** before entering the bladder above the seminal vesicle.

**Blood supply** is segmental, from renal, gonadal, aortic, common/internal iliac, vesical and uterine branches. Vessels reach the upper ureter from the **medial** side and the pelvic ureter from the **lateral** side. They form a longitudinal plexus in the adventitia.

**Nerves.** Visceral afferents enter roughly T11-L2, so pain is referred loin-to-groin.
levels.phd:
**Wall and peristalsis.** The ureter is lined by **urothelium** and has a muscularis of inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle, with an extra outer longitudinal layer in the lower third. Peristalsis is myogenic. Pacemaker activity begins in **atypical smooth muscle cells** of the renal pelvis/calyces, with hyperpolarization-activated (HCN) currents implicated. Cells expressing c-Kit (interstitial cell-like) relay the signal. Conduction passes cell to cell through gap junctions. Autonomic innervation modulates but does not initiate contractions, which is why the transplanted, denervated ureter still propels urine. Boluses move about 2-6 times per minute. At high flow the boluses merge into a continuous column.

**Development.** The ureter arises from the **ureteric bud**, an outgrowth of the mesonephric duct, around week 5. GDNF from the metanephric mesenchyme acts on RET receptors in the bud. Branching forms the pelvis, calyces and collecting ducts. Ureteric orifice position follows the **Weigert-Meyer rule**. In a complete duplication, the upper-pole ureter opens inferomedially, often ectopic or with a ureterocele. The lower-pole ureter opens superolaterally and is prone to reflux.

**Antireflux mechanics.** VUJ competence depends on the intramural tunnel length relative to ureteric diameter. A ratio of about 5:1 is the classic target from Paquin's work. The tunnel compresses against the detrusor as the bladder fills. Primary vesicoureteric reflux reflects a short tunnel. This is the logic behind reimplantation operations (e.g., Cohen cross-trigonal, Lich-Gregoir).

**Pain physiology.** Obstruction raises intraluminal pressure and stimulates local prostaglandin synthesis. This increases renal pelvic pressure and drives the colic. Pain localizes by dermatome: high obstruction gives flank pain. Lower stones refer to the groin, testis or labia via the genitofemoral and ilioinguinal territories (L1-L2). VUJ stones can mimic bladder irritation.

**Vascular nuance.** The longitudinal adventitial plexus tolerates mobilization only if the adventitia is preserved. Stripping the sheath risks ischemic stricture or fistula. The supply is weakest in the mid-ureter, which matters for transplant ureters supplied only from the renal end.
levels.expert:
**Iatrogenic injury.** Gynaecological surgery accounts for the majority of iatrogenic ureteric injuries, and colorectal and vascular surgery for many of the rest. Hot spots: the infundibulopelvic ligament at the pelvic brim, where the ureter lies just medial to the ovarian vessels during adnexal ligation; the uterine artery crossing; the vaginal cuff; and the sigmoid mesocolon in left colectomy. Many injuries are unrecognized intraoperatively and present days later with flank pain, ileus, fever, urinoma or a vaginal fistula. Prophylactic ureteric stents aid identification in hostile pelvises. They are not proven to prevent injury. Near-infrared fluorescence ureter visualization is an emerging adjunct.

**Repair by level.**
- Upper: primary ureteroureterostomy, or pyeloplasty-type repair.
- Mid: spatulated tension-free ureteroureterostomy; transureteroureterostomy is a selected option.
- Lower: ureteroneocystostomy, adding a **psoas hitch** or **Boari flap** to bridge the gap.
- Long defects: ileal ureter, buccal mucosa grafting (growing robotic experience) or autotransplantation.
Principles: debride to bleeding tissue, spatulate, close watertight over a stent, and preserve the adventitia.

**Imaging pitfalls.** Non-contrast CT is the standard for suspected stones. Phleboliths in pelvic veins mimic distal calculi. The **soft-tissue rim sign** around a stone and the **comet-tail sign** of a phlebolith help separate them. A **retrocaval (circumcaval) ureter** on the right is really a venous anomaly. It arises when the posterior cardinal vein persists, and it gives a fishhook appearance on urography.

**Neurosurgical and spinal relevance.** In anterior and lateral lumbar interbody approaches, the ureter is swept forward with the peritoneum and must be identified on psoas. Injury is rare but often missed. Peristalsis survives spinal cord injury. Bladder dysfunction, not ureteric failure, drives upper-tract damage in neurogenic bladder through high-pressure reflux.

**Pharmacology.** Ureteric smooth muscle expresses α1D/α1A adrenoceptors. That is the rationale for **medical expulsive therapy** with alpha-blockers such as tamsulosin. Large RCTs (SUSPEND, 2015) found no overall benefit, while meta-analyses suggest benefit for larger distal stones. NSAIDs treat colic by reducing prostaglandin-mediated renal pelvic pressure.

**Open questions:** the precise pacemaker ion channels, and how well fluorescence imaging reduces injury rates.

keyPoints: Ureters carry urine from renal pelvis to bladder by myogenic peristalsis
Three constrictions: pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim, vesicoureteric junction
Ureter crosses the common iliac bifurcation at the pelvic brim
Passes under the uterine artery in females and under the ductus deferens in males
Segmental blood supply: medial in the abdomen, lateral in the pelvis; protect the adventitia
Stone pain is referred loin-to-groin via roughly T11-L2

test.q: Where is the narrowest constriction of the ureter?
test.explain: The intramural vesicoureteric junction is the narrowest point and a common place for stones to lodge. Gonadal vessels cross the ureter but do not form a classic constriction.

test.q: At the pelvic brim, the ureter typically crosses the:
choices: Origin of the inferior mesenteric artery
Bifurcation of the common iliac artery
Origin of the internal pudendal artery
test.explain: The ureter enters the pelvis over the common iliac bifurcation or the start of the external iliac artery.

test.q: In the female pelvis, what passes directly above the ureter near the cervix?
test.explain: This is "water under the bridge": the ureter runs beneath the uterine artery. The ovarian vessels lie near the ureter higher up, at the brim.

test.q: In males, which structure crosses superior to the ureter before it enters the bladder?
test.explain: The ductus deferens crosses over the distal ureter, which then enters the bladder above the seminal vesicle.

test.q: How does urine move along the ureter?
test.explain: Peristaltic waves of smooth muscle propel urine, which is why flow continues even when lying down.

test.q: On which muscle does the abdominal ureter descend?
test.explain: The abdominal ureter lies on the anterior surface of psoas major.

test.q: Ureteric arteries in the pelvis approach from which side?
test.explain: Abdominal ureteric branches come from the medial side, and pelvic branches come from the lateral side, which guides safe dissection.

test.q: Ureteric colic typically spreads from the flank toward the:
test.explain: Visceral afferents enter about T11-L2, so the pain is referred loin-to-groin.

test.q: What resists reflux of urine at the vesicoureteric junction?
choices: A mucosal valve in the pelvis
test.explain: The oblique tunnel through the detrusor is compressed as the bladder fills and acts as a flap-valve.

test.q: The ureters lie behind the peritoneum, so they are described as ___.
test.explain: They are fixed behind the posterior parietal peritoneum.

test.q: What is the funnel-shaped start of the ureter inside the kidney called?
test.explain: The renal pelvis narrows into the ureter at the pelviureteric junction.

test.q: The classic phrase describing the ureter passing under the uterine artery is "water under the ___".
test.explain: Urine (water) flows under the uterine artery (the bridge).

kidTest.q: What do the ureters carry?
kidTest.explain: Ureters carry pee from the kidneys down to the bladder.

kidTest.q: How many ureters do you have?
kidTest.explain: You have one ureter for each kidney, so two in total.

kidTest.q: How does a ureter move pee along?
kidTest.explain: Its walls squeeze in waves, like pushing toothpaste along a tube.

kidTest.q: What can get stuck in the narrow spots?
kidTest.explain: Small kidney stones can get stuck where the tube is narrow.

kidTest.q: Pee goes from the kidney into the b _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The bladder stores pee until you go to the toilet.

advancedTest.q: A transplanted, denervated ureter still shows peristalsis. This best supports:
choices: Urine flow driven by bladder suction
A myogenic pacemaker in the renal pelvis
Peristalsis driven mainly by spinal reflexes
advancedTest.explain: Pacemaker cells in the pelvis/calyces initiate the waves, and autonomic nerves only modulate them.

advancedTest.q: In a complete duplex system, the Weigert-Meyer rule predicts the lower-pole ureter is prone to:
choices: Reflux due to a superolateral orifice
Retrocaval course on the right side
advancedTest.explain: The lower-pole orifice is superolateral with a short tunnel, so it refluxes. The upper-pole ureter is the one that tends to be ectopic or have a ureterocele.

advancedTest.q: Why does stripping the ureteric adventitia during mobilization risk stricture?
choices: It denervates the pacemaker and stops peristalsis
It breaks the gap junctions of the muscle
It disrupts the longitudinal arterial plexus
It removes the urothelium that blocks urine
advancedTest.explain: The segmental supply feeds an adventitial longitudinal plexus. Losing it causes ischemia, with stricture or fistula.

advancedTest.q: A gap remains after excising a distal ureteric injury, too long for direct reimplantation. A logical choice is:
advancedTest.explain: A psoas hitch (or Boari flap) brings the bladder up to bridge lower defects while keeping the repair tension-free.

lessons.title: Abdominal Aorta, IVC and the Left Renal Vein

levels.kid:
Inside your belly, near your backbone, run two giant tubes side by side. They are like the biggest highways in a city.

The **aorta** is on the left side. It carries fresh red blood down from your heart. Along the way it sends off smaller roads to your tummy, your kidneys and your legs.

The **vena cava** is on the right side. It carries used blood back up to your heart. It is wider and softer.

The vein from your left kidney has a long trip. It has to cross over to reach the vena cava. It passes through a narrow gap between the aorta and another tube, like a car going under a low bridge. If the gap gets too tight, the vein can get squeezed.
levels.hs:
The **abdominal aorta** is the main artery of the abdomen. It enters the abdomen through the **aortic hiatus** of the diaphragm at about the level of the 12th thoracic vertebra (T12). It runs down just left of the midline, in front of the vertebral bodies. At about L4 it splits into the two **common iliac arteries**, which supply the pelvis and legs.

Its branches come in three groups:
- **Unpaired gut branches** to the digestive tract: the celiac trunk, the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).
- **Paired visceral branches** to the adrenals, kidneys and gonads.
- **Wall branches** to the diaphragm and the lumbar region.

The **inferior vena cava (IVC)** is the large vein that returns blood from the lower body. It forms at about L5, where the common iliac veins join. It runs up to the right of the aorta and passes through the diaphragm at T8.

The **left renal vein** is much longer than the right one, because the IVC sits on the right side of the body. To reach the IVC, it crosses in front of the aorta, just below where the SMA begins. When the SMA and the aorta squeeze this vein, the problem is called **nutcracker syndrome**.
levels.college:
**Abdominal aorta.** It enters through the aortic hiatus at T12, behind the median arcuate ligament. It descends retroperitoneally, to the left of the midline, on the lumbar vertebral bodies, and bifurcates at L4. The bifurcation projects roughly onto the umbilicus and the supracristal plane. Its branches are:
- **Anterior, unpaired:** celiac trunk (T12), SMA (L1) and IMA (L3).
- **Lateral, paired:** middle suprarenal arteries, renal arteries (L1–L2) and gonadal arteries (L2).
- **Posterolateral:** the inferior phrenic arteries and four pairs of lumbar arteries.
- **Terminal:** the common iliac arteries and the small median sacral artery.

The right renal artery is longer and passes **behind the IVC**.

**IVC.** It forms at L5, behind the right common iliac artery, and ascends on the right. It lies on the right crus and the right sympathetic trunk. It grooves the bare area of the liver and pierces the central tendon at T8. Its tributaries are the common iliacs, the lumbar veins, the right gonadal vein, both renal veins, the right suprarenal vein, the inferior phrenic veins and the hepatic veins. It receives no veins from the gut, because that blood drains through the portal system.

**Left renal vein.** It is about three times longer than the right. It runs in front of the aorta, in the angle below the SMA origin, and ends in the IVC at about L1. On its way it receives three tributaries:
- the **left gonadal vein**, entering at a right angle;
- the **left suprarenal vein**;
- often a **lumbar or hemiazygos connection** (the renal-azygos-lumbar trunk).

**Clinical anchors:**
- Compression between the SMA and the aorta causes **nutcracker syndrome**, with blood in the urine, flank pain and a left varicocele.
- The same SMA–aorta angle can compress the third part of the duodenum (**SMA syndrome**).
- A left varicocele that appears suddenly in an adult can signal a left renal tumour blocking the vein.
levels.expert:
**Aneurysm surgery.** Most abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) are infrarenal. The proximal **neck** dominates endovascular planning: its length (usually at least 10–15 mm is needed), its angulation and the presence of thrombus decide whether a standard endograft can seal. Short necks need fenestrated or branched grafts, or chimney techniques that preserve the renal arteries and the SMA.

**Renal vein variants in open repair.** In open repair the left renal vein crosses the operative field at the neck. It can be divided close to the IVC with acceptable outcomes in many patients, because gonadal, suprarenal and lumbar collaterals keep draining the kidney. This works only if those tributaries are preserved. A retroaortic or circumaortic vein, if not recognised on preoperative CT, is a classic source of catastrophic bleeding when the surgeon clamps or dissects behind the aorta.

**IVC pathology and access.**
- Retroperitoneal sarcomas, leiomyosarcoma of the IVC and renal cell carcinoma can extend into the vein as tumour thrombus. The **Neves (Mayo) levels**, from the renal vein up to the right atrium, guide whether the case needs caval control alone, liver mobilisation or cardiopulmonary bypass.
- IVC filters are usually placed infrarenally. A duplicated IVC risks failure unless both limbs are addressed.

**Spine surgery relevance.** For a neurosurgery-oriented learner, anterior and lateral lumbar interbody fusion (ALIF, LLIF) requires mobilising the aorta, the IVC and the iliac vessels. The left common iliac vein is especially vulnerable at L4–L5. The **iliolumbar vein** is tethered and must be ligated to retract the vein safely. Vascular injury rates in ALIF are reported at roughly 1–15%, and most of these injuries are venous.

**May–Thurner anatomy.** The right common iliac artery compresses the left common iliac vein against L5. This predisposes to left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, and treatment is now usually venous stenting.

**Open questions.**
- Optimal treatment of nutcracker syndrome is debated. Options include renal vein transposition, external stenting and endovascular stenting, which carries a risk of stent migration.
- Normative aortomesenteric criteria in adolescents are poorly defined.
- Whether AAA screening programmes still give a net benefit as prevalence falls is under re-evaluation.

keyPoints: The aorta enters at T12 and bifurcates at L4; the IVC forms at L5 and leaves at T8
Unpaired gut branches: celiac (T12), SMA (L1), IMA (L3)
The IVC lies right of the aorta, so the right renal artery passes behind it
The left renal vein crosses in front of the aorta, below the SMA origin
The left gonadal and left suprarenal veins drain into the left renal vein
SMA–aorta compression of the left renal vein causes nutcracker syndrome

test.q: At what vertebral level does the abdominal aorta usually bifurcate?
test.explain: The aorta divides into the common iliac arteries at about L4. T12 is where it enters the abdomen.

test.q: The IVC passes through the diaphragm at which level?
test.explain: The IVC pierces the central tendon at T8. The aorta passes at T12 and the esophagus at T10.

test.q: Which branch of the aorta arises at about L3?
test.explain: The IMA arises at about L3. The celiac trunk arises at T12 and the SMA at L1.

test.q: Why is the left renal vein longer than the right?
choices: The IVC lies to the right
test.explain: The IVC is on the right, so the left renal vein has to cross the midline to reach it.

test.q: The left renal vein crosses which structure on its way to the IVC?
test.explain: It passes in front of the aorta and just below the SMA origin, which is why the two arteries can squeeze it.

test.q: Which renal vessel passes behind the IVC?
test.explain: The aorta lies to the left of the IVC, so the right renal artery must pass behind the IVC to reach the right kidney.

test.q: The left gonadal vein usually drains into the:
test.explain: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein. The right gonadal vein drains directly into the IVC.

test.q: Which set of findings fits nutcracker syndrome?
choices: Pain after meals and weight loss
Blood in the urine and a left varicocele
Vomiting and an upper bowel blockage
Leg swelling from iliac vein compression
test.explain: Compression of the left renal vein causes haematuria and flank pain, and backs up the gonadal vein, causing a left varicocele. Vomiting from a blocked duodenum fits SMA syndrome instead.

test.q: Why does the IVC receive no veins from the gut?
choices: Gut blood drains via the portal vein
Gut blood enters the renal veins
Gut blood enters the lumbar veins
Gut blood drains to the azygos
test.explain: Venous blood from the gut flows through the portal system to the liver, and only then reaches the IVC through the hepatic veins.

test.q: The aorta enters the abdomen through the aortic ___ at T12.
test.explain: The aortic hiatus lies behind the median arcuate ligament.

test.q: Two veins join at L5 to form the IVC. Name them.
test.explain: The left and right common iliac veins unite at L5 to form the IVC.

test.q: Compression of the left renal vein between the SMA and the aorta is called ___ syndrome.
test.explain: The two arteries act like the arms of a nutcracker on the vein.

kidTest.q: What does the aorta carry?
choices: Used blood back to the heart
kidTest.explain: The aorta carries fresh blood away from the heart.

kidTest.q: Which way does the vena cava carry blood?
kidTest.explain: The vena cava brings used blood back up to the heart.

kidTest.q: Which kidney's vein has the longer trip?
kidTest.explain: The left kidney's vein has to cross over to reach the vena cava on the right.

kidTest.q: Where do the two big tubes run?
kidTest.explain: They run deep in the belly, next to the backbone.

kidTest.q: The big artery from the heart is the a _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The aorta is the body's biggest artery.

advancedTest.q: During open AAA repair the left renal vein is divided near the IVC. Why does the kidney usually survive?
choices: The portal vein takes over its outflow
The renal artery carries the venous blood back out
The right renal vein drains both kidneys
advancedTest.explain: If the gonadal, suprarenal and lumbar tributaries are preserved, they drain the kidney. Dividing the vein farther out, beyond these tributaries, would remove that safety net.

advancedTest.q: Preoperative CT shows a retroaortic left renal vein. Which open-surgery step carries the highest risk?
choices: Opening the sac below the bifurcation
Dissecting or clamping behind the aorta
advancedTest.explain: A retroaortic vein runs behind the aorta, so dissecting or clamping there can tear it and cause catastrophic bleeding.

advancedTest.q: A thin, symptom-free teenager has a narrow SMA–aorta angle on CT. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Compression on imaging is often benign
Pressure gradients have no added value
It suggests that the IVC is duplicated
advancedTest.explain: Anatomical compression is common in people without symptoms, especially thin adolescents. The diagnosis needs symptoms plus haemodynamic evidence, such as a raised renocaval pressure gradient.

advancedTest.q: A man in his 50s suddenly develops a left varicocele. Which explanation is most likely?
choices: May–Thurner compression of the iliac vein
A defective valve in the right gonadal vein
A left renal mass blocking venous outflow
advancedTest.explain: The left gonadal vein drains into the left renal vein. A new varicocele in an adult can signal a renal tumour blocking that vein.

lessons.title: Posterior Wall Muscles and the Lumbar Plexus

levels.kid:
Imagine the back wall of your tummy is like the back wall of a room. Behind your belly organs there are strong muscles that hold you up and help you bend and lift your legs.

One muscle is called the **psoas** (say "SO-us"). It runs from your backbone down to the top of your leg. It helps you lift your knee, like when you march or climb stairs.

Inside and around these muscles runs a bundle of **nerves**, like electric wires in a wall. This bundle is called the **lumbar plexus**. Its wires carry messages to your hips, your belly skin and the front of your legs. They tell your muscles to move, and they tell your brain when something touches your skin.
levels.hs:
The **posterior abdominal wall** is the back wall of the abdomen, lying behind the kidneys and other retroperitoneal organs. It is built from four main muscles:
- **Psoas major**: a long muscle running from the lumbar vertebrae (T12 to L5) down to the femur (thigh bone). It **flexes the hip**, meaning it lifts the thigh forward.
- **Iliacus**: a fan-shaped muscle lining the inside of the hip bone. It joins psoas, and together they are called **iliopsoas**, the strongest hip flexor.
- **Quadratus lumborum**: a flat, square muscle between the 12th rib and the top of the pelvis. It bends the trunk sideways and steadies the 12th rib when you breathe.
- The back parts of the **diaphragm** also form the top of this wall.

A **plexus** is a network where nerves join and swap fibers. The **lumbar plexus** forms from the front branches of spinal nerves **L1 to L4** and is built inside the psoas muscle. Its branches include the **femoral nerve**, which powers the quadriceps (the knee-straightening muscles), and the **obturator nerve**, which supplies the inner-thigh muscles.

Real example: in **appendicitis**, an inflamed appendix can rest on the right psoas. Stretching the hip backward then hurts. Doctors call this the **psoas sign**.
levels.college:
**Muscles of the posterior abdominal wall**
- **Psoas major**: arises from the sides of the T12 to L5 vertebral bodies, their intervertebral discs and the transverse processes. It descends along the pelvic brim, passes under the inguinal ligament and inserts on the **lesser trochanter** of the femur. It is innervated by the anterior rami of **L1 to L3**.
- **Psoas minor**: present in only about 40 to 60% of people. It runs from T12 and L1 to the iliopubic eminence.
- **Iliacus**: arises from the iliac fossa and joins the psoas tendon. It is supplied by the femoral nerve.
- **Quadratus lumborum (QL)**: runs from the iliac crest and iliolumbar ligament to the 12th rib and the L1 to L4 transverse processes. It is supplied by T12 to L4. It flexes the trunk laterally and anchors the 12th rib during inspiration.

The diaphragm's **medial and lateral arcuate ligaments** arch over the psoas and QL. These muscles are wrapped in fascia continuous with the transversalis fascia (the **psoas fascia** and the anterior layer of the thoracolumbar fascia).

**Lumbar plexus (L1 to L4, often with T12)** forms within psoas. A useful order is "I twice get lunch on Fridays":
- **Iliohypogastric (L1)** and **ilioinguinal (L1)**: emerge at the lateral border of psoas, run across the QL and supply the lower abdominal muscles and the skin of the groin and anterior genitals.
- **Genitofemoral (L1, L2)**: pierces the front of psoas. Its genital branch supplies the cremaster muscle; its femoral branch supplies the skin of the upper thigh.
- **Lateral femoral cutaneous (L2, L3)**: passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine.
- **Obturator (L2 to L4)**: emerges at the medial border of psoas and supplies the adductors.
- **Femoral (L2 to L4)**: emerges laterally between psoas and iliacus and supplies the quadriceps, iliacus and anterior thigh skin.

The **lumbosacral trunk (L4, L5)** passes medially to join the sacral plexus.
levels.phd:
**Topographic logic.** The lumbar plexus assembles from anterior rami within the substance of psoas major, between its superficial layer (arising from the vertebral bodies and discs) and its deep layer (arising from the transverse processes). This intramuscular origin explains the exit pattern. Only the **genitofemoral nerve** pierces the anterior surface of psoas. The **obturator nerve** and the **lumbosacral trunk** emerge medially. All the other branches emerge laterally. Each ramus divides into anterior and posterior divisions, just as the brachial plexus does. Anterior divisions of L2 to L4 form the obturator nerve, which supplies the adductor (ventral, flexor-derived) compartment. Posterior divisions of L2 to L4 form the femoral nerve, which supplies the extensor-derived quadriceps. This mirrors the dorsal and ventral muscle mass split seen in limb-bud development. An **accessory obturator nerve** (L3, L4) occurs in roughly 10 to 30% of people. It crosses the superior pubic ramus rather than passing through the obturator canal.

**Psoas morphology and function.** Psoas major shows marked intersubject variation in cross-sectional area and fiber type. Electromyography (EMG) studies show it acts mainly as a hip flexor. Its lumbar segments contribute modest axial compression and stiffening, with little true lumbar flexion moment. Bogduk's anatomical modeling argued that psoas has a poor lever arm for moving lumbar segments. That conclusion challenges the older teaching that psoas tightness drives lumbar hyperlordosis.

**Fascial compartments.** The psoas fascia forms a closed tube from the medial arcuate ligament down to the lesser trochanter. As a result, pus from vertebral or retroperitoneal sources tracks along psoas into the femoral triangle. Classically this is a tuberculous **cold abscess** arising from spinal tuberculosis (Pott disease). QL is enclosed between the anterior and middle layers of the thoracolumbar fascia. Debate about how injectate spreads through these layers, toward the paravertebral space, underlies controversy over regional anesthesia.

**Vascular relations.** Lumbar arteries arise from the aorta and pass behind the psoas tendinous arches. The **ascending lumbar veins** link the lumbar veins to the azygos and hemiazygos systems, forming a caval bypass pathway. The **iliolumbar artery** supplies psoas, iliacus and QL.
levels.expert:
**Lateral transpsoas spine surgery (LLIF/XLIF).** The lateral approach reaches the L1 to L5 discs through psoas, so it places the lumbar plexus directly at risk. Anatomical studies by Uribe, and by Benglis and colleagues, defined **safe zones** on lateral imaging. The plexus migrates from posterior to anterior as it descends. As a result, the safe corridor narrows at **L4 to L5**, where the femoral nerve lies close to the middle of the disc. That level is often blocked by a high iliac crest as well. After surgery, transient anterior thigh numbness or hip flexor weakness is common. Most of it comes from psoas trauma or genitofemoral irritation. True femoral nerve palsy, with quadriceps weakness and loss of the patellar reflex, is less common but disabling. Directional triggered EMG and saphenous somatosensory evoked potentials reduce the risk, but they are no guarantee. Retractor time is a modifiable factor. The **oblique (pre-psoas, OLIF/ATP)** corridor between the aorta and psoas avoids the muscle. In exchange, it carries risks to the sympathetic chain, the ureter and the vessels.

**Diagnostic pitfalls.**
- **Retroperitoneal hematoma**, for example during anticoagulation or after femoral access, can compress the femoral nerve within the iliacus compartment. It presents with groin pain, a flexed hip and quadriceps weakness. Getting imaging promptly matters.
- **Meralgia paresthetica** is entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve near the anterior superior iliac spine. It is sensory only, which distinguishes it from L2 to L3 radiculopathy.
- **Ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerve injury** after inguinal hernia repair or a Pfannenstiel incision is a classic cause of chronic groin pain. Treatment options include neurectomy.
- **Lumbar plexopathy**, as in diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy, mimics a radiculopathy. Electromyography of the paraspinal muscles helps tell them apart: those muscles are typically normal when the lesion is in the plexus.

**Anesthesia.** The **quadratus lumborum block**, described by Blanco, and the **fascia iliaca block** target these fascial planes. Studies with cadavers and imaging disagree about how far injectate spreads toward the paravertebral space. This leaves unresolved how much the blocks relieve visceral, as opposed to somatic, pain. Unintended femoral nerve spread from a QL block can cause quadriceps weakness and falls.

**Frontier.** Psoas cross-sectional area on CT is a validated marker of **sarcopenia**. It predicts complications and mortality after major surgery, though measurement standards still vary.

keyPoints: Psoas major, iliacus and quadratus lumborum form the posterior abdominal wall
Iliopsoas inserts on the lesser trochanter and is the main hip flexor
The lumbar plexus (L1 to L4) forms inside psoas major
Genitofemoral pierces psoas; obturator emerges medially; most others emerge laterally
Femoral nerve (posterior divisions L2 to L4) supplies quadriceps; obturator (anterior divisions) supplies adductors
Psoas abscesses track to the thigh, and lateral transpsoas surgery risks the plexus

test.q: Which spinal nerve levels mainly form the lumbar plexus?
test.explain: The lumbar plexus arises from the anterior rami of L1 to L4, often with a contribution from T12. L4 to S3 belongs to the sacral plexus.

test.q: Within which muscle does the lumbar plexus form?
test.explain: The plexus assembles inside psoas major, between its superficial and deep layers.

test.q: Where does iliopsoas insert?
test.explain: Iliopsoas inserts on the lesser trochanter. The greater trochanter receives the gluteal muscles.

test.q: Which nerve pierces the anterior surface of psoas major?
test.explain: The genitofemoral nerve is the branch that pierces the front of psoas.

test.q: Which nerve emerges from the medial border of psoas?
test.explain: The obturator nerve and the lumbosacral trunk emerge medially. Most other branches emerge laterally.

test.q: The femoral nerve mainly supplies which muscle group?
test.explain: The femoral nerve (L2 to L4) powers the quadriceps. The obturator nerve supplies the adductors.

test.q: A main action of quadratus lumborum is to:
test.explain: QL bends the trunk laterally and steadies the 12th rib during breathing.

test.q: Pain on stretching the right hip backward in appendicitis is called the:
test.explain: An inflamed appendix lying on the psoas causes pain when the muscle is stretched. This is the psoas sign.

test.q: Why can a vertebral abscess appear in the groin or upper thigh?
choices: Pus tracks within the psoas fascia
Lymph carries it to the knee
test.explain: The psoas fascia forms a tube running down to the lesser trochanter, so pus tracks into the femoral triangle.

test.q: What is the combined name for psoas major and iliacus?
test.explain: The two muscles share a tendon and act together as iliopsoas, the strongest hip flexor.

test.q: The lumbosacral ___, carrying fibers from L4 and L5, joins the sacral plexus.
test.explain: The lumbosacral trunk links the lumbar and sacral plexuses.

test.q: Which nerve, entrapped near the anterior superior iliac spine, causes meralgia paresthetica? (give its full name)
test.explain: Entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve causes numbness and burning in the lateral thigh without weakness.

kidTest.q: What does the psoas muscle help you do?
kidTest.explain: The psoas runs from the backbone to the leg and lifts the knee.

kidTest.q: What is the lumbar plexus like?
kidTest.explain: It's a bundle of nerves that carries messages, like wires in a wall.

kidTest.q: Where are these muscles found?
choices: At the tips of the fingers
Inside the top of the head
At the back wall of the tummy
kidTest.explain: They form the back wall behind the belly organs.

kidTest.q: The nerves of the lumbar plexus go to which body part?
kidTest.explain: They carry messages to the hips, belly skin and the front of the legs.

kidTest.q: The muscle that runs from your backbone to your leg is the p _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The psoas (say SO-us) helps lift the thigh.

advancedTest.q: Why is the L4 to L5 level the riskiest for a lateral transpsoas approach?
choices: The aorta divides into two iliac arteries directly at that disc
The psoas muscle ends above L4, which exposes the nerve roots
The genitofemoral nerve exits the spinal canal at that level
The plexus lies more anteriorly there, crossing the disc's middle
advancedTest.explain: The plexus migrates anteriorly as it descends, so the safe corridor narrows at L4 to L5, often with a high iliac crest as well.

advancedTest.q: The femoral and obturator nerves supply different thigh compartments because they arise from:
choices: Different spinal levels with no overlap between them
Separate layers of quadratus lumborum during development
Posterior and anterior divisions of the L2 to L4 rami
Sympathetic and somatic fibers mixing within the psoas
advancedTest.explain: The posterior divisions form the femoral nerve, which supplies extensor-derived muscles. The anterior divisions form the obturator nerve, which supplies flexor-derived adductors. Both share L2 to L4.

advancedTest.q: A patient with weakness of thigh flexion and adduction has normal paraspinal EMG. This favors:
choices: Meralgia paresthetica at the inguinal ligament
L3 root compression by a disc herniation
A lesion confined to the femoral nerve
A lesion of the lumbar plexus
advancedTest.explain: Normal paraspinals point to a lesion beyond the root. Involvement of both the femoral and obturator territories implicates the plexus, not a single nerve.

advancedTest.q: Bogduk's modeling challenged the idea that a tight psoas drives lumbar hyperlordosis because psoas:
choices: Attaches mainly to the lumbar transverse processes
Has a poor lever arm on lumbar segments
Is supplied by sacral rather than lumbar nerves
Relaxes fully whenever the hip is being flexed
advancedTest.explain: Psoas lines up close to the lumbar axes of rotation. It mainly compresses and stiffens the spine rather than producing large lumbar flexion or extension moments.
